pages.text: Digitized by Arya Samaj Foundation Chennai and eGangotri ` INTRODUCTION Bhava Prakasa is an important treatise on Ayurveda, being counted as one of the "Laghu Trayi" (little three classical texts). It continues to be studied by students and practitioners alike, since a long time. Author In the invocatory verse the author gives his name as Bhava misra! and in the colophon of each chapter, mentions his father's name as Latakana mišra*. Apart from these two names he has not furnished any information about his date, province he belonged to, place of residence, professional and literary activities etc. in this book. Three more books written by him are krown but are not available in print. Whether these contain any of his whereabouts is also not known. So what we now know about him definitely is very little. ; | From a critical study of the present text and other relevent literature, modern scholars have arrived at the following "most likely assumptions." * 1. Bhāvamišra was an orthodox Brahmin—his surname "migra" being used especially by brahmins only, his reverential mentioning ofthe names of many Hindu gods such as Brahma, Visnu (Sripati, Madhusudana Hari), Mahešvara (Hara, Siva) Ganeš Surya, Agni (pavaka) Hanumanita, Angàraka, Gaūgā, Bhūdevatās (brahmanas) etc. 2. He belonged to Magadha (south Bihar) since he gives the names of many kinds of menu (cooked foods) known only in Magadha (lower and middle parts of Bihar)’. 3. His place of residence was Gaya according to Priyavrat sharma‘. Kānyakubja according to Gananath sen5. and Banaras, according to Julius jolly* and others. Further research only can confirm the correct place, 4. He was an independent medical practitioner since he does not make mention of any king or chieftain-either Hindu or Muslim as his patron or benefactor. Date The following points form the basis for determining his date— 1. The last text from which Bhāvamišra has quoted is Madanapala Nighantu. This was complete in 1347 A.D. (14th cent. A.D.). So this will be the upper limit for the date of Bhavamisra. 2. Yogaratnakara and Vaidyajivana (Lolambarājīya) both texts belonging to 1. Bhāvaprakaša is the first text of Ayurveda to describe phirafiga roga (syphilis) and suggest chopcini (similax china/china root) as a remedy for it. Phiranga roga came to India through the Portugeese and the French in 15th Cent A.D. It was in 16th Cent. only it spread widely forcing patients to seek medical aid. Texts of Ayurveda, Unani and other medical systems written during or after 16th cent. A.D. only contain detailed description of this disease and its treatment. Considering all these points Bhāvamišra is placed in 16th Cent. A.D. without much doubt. Works Four books written by Bhāva migra have been known so far-viz1. Bhāva prakāša-probably his first work now available in full along with a commentary in Sanskrit. Both printed. 2. Gunaratnamala-Mss. available!. 3. Madhava nidāna tippani-Mss. available. 4. Vaidyanighantu-not traced so far”. Bhava Praka$a— nature and scope Bhava Prakāša is comprehensive in nature containing all important aspects of Ayurveda-doctrinal and applied-blended together. The author himself has stated at the outset that very important informations and efficacious medicinal recipes have been collected from many reputed ancient texts and put in his book*. The book is composed entirely in Sanskrit verses of different metres. It is needless to say that many verses of other texts have been incorporated, sources of many such borrowings mentioned either in the text or in the commentary. The text has about 10268 verses, in total”, distributed among three khandas (sections), seven bhagas (parts) and 80 prakaranas (chapters); some chapters have subchapters also as shown below : I. pages.text: Digitized by Arya Samaj Foundation Chennai and eGangotri 10 BHAVAPRAKASA-PURVAKHANDA Contents in brief Cn Š Pūrva khanda (first section) has seven chapters and deals with origin of Ayurvedachief gods and sages propogating it— Lokasrsti-paficabhuta triguna-Atma; Ifidriyamanas; Garbhotpatti—Sarira aūga-avayava-Dosādi vijūana-Dinacaryā-rtucaryāsadācāra-rogakāraņa-cikitsāpāda Sadrasa gunakarma—Ausadha dravyas-sangrahan apratinidhi-ausadha ahara dravya varga (groups of drugs and articles of dieti bhāga). e different groups of drugs and articles of diet is dealt in 24 (twenty four) vargas (groups) which form part of chapter 6 is considered the speciality of Bhavaprakasa. The author frunishes names, synonyms, names in different regions, properties and actions, tests, etc. of drugs of all categories (vegetable, animal and mineral origin). Apart from the drugs which are in use since long, many new ones which have come to India through western countries and those used in Unani system of medicine have also been incorporated in this text. Hence Bhavamišra is given the credit for enlarging the materia medica of Ayurveda with addition of new drugs. This portion of the text is known popularly as Bhāvaprakāša nighantu and has been published seperately with detailed notes by many present day scholars!. Madhya Khanda— Middle/ second section has 7] chapters dealing with the nidana (aetiology), laksana (symptomatology), samprapti (pathogenesis) sadhyasadhyata (prognosis) and cikitsā (treatment) of all diseases, with greater emphasis on Kaya cikitsa (inner medicine). Both Kasthausadha (formulae from vegetable drugs) and Rasausadha (formulae from mercury and minerals) are mentioned in the treatment. Uttara Khanda— Third and last section has only two chapters, one dealing with Vajikarana cikitsā (virilification therapy) and the other with Rasayana cikitsā (rejuvinatory therapy). Commentaries— Till now only two commentaries in Sanskrit on Bhavaprakasa are known— 1. First one— which has no specific name is available in full and printed along with the text. 2. Second commentary by name "Sadvaidya siddhāīta ratnakara" is written by Jayadeva, son of Jayakrisna on the orders of Maharaja Ranavira Simha, king of Kashmir’. This is incomplete and its manuscript is in the library of Jammu’. Regarding the first commentary available now, there are doubts about its authorship among the present day scholars, since there is no mention in it. Some scholars opine that Bhavamiéra the author of the text is also the commentator; some others say, the traditional belief is that Bhāvamišra wrote only a tippani (short notes/ gloss) and not an eloborate commentary like the one now available; yet others hold the view that the commentator is a person different from Bhavamisra and has chosen to remain incognito. == AM 1. pages.text: Digitized by Arya Samaj Foundation Chennai and eGangotri INTRODUCTION 11 I am of the opinion that Bhāvamišra himself is the author of the commentory also, as can be inferred from his own words!. The use of the words 'Vyakhyana' in this sentence makes it clear that what he wrote is 'vyakhyana’ (commentary) only and not tippani-gloss/short notes. The commentary is neither too eloborate nor too brief, written in simple language and lucid style, furnishes quotations from other treatises mentioning their source, especially of the numerous medicinal formulae. It also explains many moot and doubtful points mentioned in the text, gives additional information about drugs and practice in vogue of preparing medicinal formulae and usage etc. Thus the commentary is very valuable and greatly helpful to understand the original text. Editions and translations i The first edition of Bhāvaprakāša-full text together with its commentary was edited and published by Sri Jīvananda vidyasagar Bhattacharya, Calcutta in 1875. This was the authentic copy of the manuscript and so considered as authoritative. Since then it has been published many times, edited by different scholars; some edītors have published the nighaņtu portion of the text only under the name Bhāvaprakāša Nighaņtu*. Bhāvaprakāša has been translated into Hindi and some other Indian languages, but not to any foreign language so far. This translation into English is the first in this category. Similar to my translation of other Āyurveda texts, this also is faithful to the original, reliaing on its commentary for the meaning of difficult words. I feel my labours amply rewarded if it can render an iota of help to students and practitioners of Āyurveda to understand and appreciate Bhāvaprakāša. I have dedicated this volume to the memory of my preceptor Prof. M. Visvanatha Dvivedi. He was my teacher of Dravyaguņavijīīāna (Pharmacology and materia medica) at the Post-graduate centre (now Gujarat Ayurveda University) Jamnagar during 1956-58. He was a great scholar in many subjects of Ayurveda, especially of Dravyaguna vijūāna. A prolific writer he has authored more than two dozen books, appreciated by teachers and students alike. Bhavaprakasa Nighantu edited by him with copius supplementary notes is a monumental contribution. His lectures were full of experience and highly beneficial. These have made me and my classmates indebted to him. This dediction is a small token of my reverence to my preceptor. Ere concluding, I convery my hearty thanks to Sri. G. Mahesh. pages.text: Digitized by Arya Samaj Foundation Chennai and eGangotri BHAVAPRAKASA-PURVAKHANDA qia sat: NT a: | NĒ aasiitisrm ARN RS N Once, the worshipful sage, Atreya, feeling for the difficulties of the people of . the world suffering from diseases pondered over—"What shall I do? Where shall I . go? How can I make this world free from disease? I cannot see them suffer, I am of very kind heart, hence it is very painful for my heart also. So I will study Ayurveda for ' making people of the world free from pain (disease). Deciding thus, sage Atreya went to heaven. = There he saw Lord Ifdra, the lord of the gods and the great master of Ayurveda seated on the throne, praised by the gods and sages, shining like the sun illuminating all the quarters. y Iüdra as soon as he saw him (Atreya) descended from the throne and worshipped him first, who was worn out by severe penances, enquired about his welfare and the reason for his coming. Then the sage began to explain the reasons for his . coming in this manner. Oh! Devaraja! you are not the lord of only the heaven, since Vidhata (Brahma) - has made you the protector of all the three worlds; in the world of the earth, people are sufferihg from diseases, and their mind full of grief. So bestow your grace for them, teach me Ayurveda, out of compasion towards men. Indra, agreed to this request and taught the sage. The great sage having learnt Ayurveda in full, blessed the lord with many benedictions and returned to the earth. These are material substances having pramana (quantity), guna (qualities/properties) and karma (functions). Each of these has a normal limit in respect of its quantity, qualities and functions. This normalcy (prakria) is conducive for maintaince of health (ārogya). This normalcy of dosas is not stable and undergoes change either to vrddhi (increase) or ksaya/ksina (decrease) by the effect of age, climate, season, day and night, food and activities of men. Increase or decrease are both vikyta (abnormal). Such abnormalcy may be in respect of either pramana (quantity), guna (qualities) or karma (functions) or all together. Abnormalcy of dosas (dosa vaisamya) is not conducive for health but gives rise to diseases. Mild degree of abnormalcy is constantly going on due to the effect of climate, food and activities which are unavoidable and the body will have become accustomed to it. On the other hand great degree of abnormalcy which occurs as a result of unhealthy and unaccustomed food, improper food habits, abnormal kinds of activites etc. brings about great changes in the tissues of the body and gives rise to diseases. pages.text: R ns n cene MEM oe Ps < "ygitized'iy Arya Samaj Foundation Chennat and eGangotri | f - — Fa out the Book: Bhāvaprakāša written by Bhāvamišra is an authoritative text on Ayurveda and is being studied by students, teachers and practitioners of Ayurveda since last five centuries. It is comprehensive, dealing with basic doctrines, aetiology, symptomatology and treatment of all diseases. It describes about 500 drugs belonging to vegetable, mineral and animal kingdoms. This lexicon of drugs (Nighantu Bhāga) is considered as a speciality of this text since it incorporates many new drugs unknown in the ancient period. In the treatment of diseases both Kāsthausadhas (Vegetable drugs) and Rasausadhas (mercurial and mineral drugs) have been prescribed. With all these merits Bhāvaprakāša has been a very popular text. Need for its English translation was being keenly felt specially by Post-graduate students. This translation is a step in that direction. Sait ; The translator Prof. Srikantha Murthy is person rich in experience of teaching Ayurveda and writing valuable books. His earlier translations into English of Šārangadhara Samhita, Madhava Nidāna, Astānga Hrdaya and Astanga Sarngraha have earned for him an international reputation. This book is the next in that series. Bhàvapraka$a— complete treatise—is proposed to be published in two volumes. Vol. I—Prathama Khanda including Nighantu bhaga. Vol. H— Madhya and Uttara Khanda. Each volume will have many appendeces and index—prepared so as to be very useful for all Ayurvedists. - ee oS NOS X DRAVYAGUNA VIJNANA oe (ENGLISH—SANSERIT ) MATERIA MEDICA - VEGETABLE DRUGS (PART I :A - J) By: Dr. Gyanendra Pandey This work deals with indigenous materia medica, pharmacology and therapeutics of Ayurveda, with special reference to drug obtained from vegetable origin or the plant drugs belonging to Indian medical science. It is the first work of-its kind, fulfilling the need and demand in India and abroad. The work is in English language supported with Sanskrit texts (with proper references/ contexts). Present volume is presented as part 1 as opening volume of the work in series (planned to be brought out in three volumes). This volume 1 contains about 150 drugs covering A to J. The work covers all the relevant aspects of drugs generally dealt in the sphere of Dravyaguna _ Vijūāna or Indian materia medica. Being the first volume, its section 1 deals the classification (gana, ~~ varga etc.) of drugs and main section II entirely covers individual drugs which are to continue in further volumes. The glossary of technical and medical terms related to drugs and Dravyaguna Vijnana is given; and the indices of botanical and Sanskrit names alongwith other lists have been provi ed. The subject matter drugs and topics as required in the subject-course of Dravyaguņa Vijūāna under curriculum of Central Council of Indian Medicine and other studies needs have been kept in view.
